gain-staging.description: Essential gain staging guidelines for Hardcore to prevent clipping and maintain headroom

rules.title: Maintain Unity Gain Principle
rules.description: When toggling effects on/off, perceived loudness should remain consistent
rules.details: If an effect makes the track louder when enabled, reduce its output level or the mix control. This ensures you're making tonal decisions, not just liking something because it's louder.
rules.check: A/B test with effect on/off at same perceived volume
rules.violation: Effect sounds better simply because it's louder
rules.solution: Adjust Level/Makeup/Mix controls to match dry signal volume

rules.title: Input Gain Sets the Foundation
rules.description: Input gain determines how hard the first stompbox is driven
rules.details: Higher input gain = more saturation in distortion pedals. Start at 0dB and adjust based on your source level and desired saturation amount.
rules.check: Input meter shows healthy level without constant red
rules.solution: Reduce input gain or source track volume

rules.title: Cumulative Gain Across Chain
rules.description: Each stompbox adds or reduces gain. Monitor cumulative effect.
rules.details: Distortion adds gain, compression adds makeup gain, EQ boosts add gain. Stack multiple gain-increasing effects and you'll run out of headroom.
rules.check: Master output meter stays below 0dBFS
rules.formula: Input + Stompbox gains + Master EQ boosts < 0dBFS
rules.violation: Master output clipping despite individual effects not clipping
rules.solution: Reduce individual effect output levels or enable master limiter

rules.title: Distortion Level Compensation
rules.description: Distortion increases perceived loudness due to added harmonics
rules.details: Even if peak levels don't increase, distortion adds high-frequency content that sounds louder. Compensate by reducing Distortion Level control.
rules.check: Loudness meter (LUFS) comparison with/without distortion
rules.violation: Distortion sounds 'better' but is actually just louder
rules.solution: Reduce Distortion Level by 10-20% or use mix control

rules.title: Compressor Makeup Gain Math
rules.description: Set makeup gain to compensate for gain reduction
rules.details: If compressor is reducing gain by 6dB on average, set makeup gain to approximately +6dB. Over-compensation causes clipping; under-compensation makes track too quiet.
rules.check: Output level matches input level (bypass test)
rules.violation: Compressed signal significantly louder or quieter than dry
rules.solution: Adjust Makeup Gain to match GR meter average

rules.title: EQ Boost Gain Compensation
rules.description: Boosting frequencies adds gain at those frequencies
rules.details: +6dB boost at 3kHz increases the overall level if that frequency was present. Compensate with output gain reduction if multiple boosts applied.
rules.check: Master output after EQ stays at healthy level
rules.rule: Sum of all EQ boosts should not exceed +12dB without compensation
rules.solution: Cut instead of boost, or reduce master output gain

rules.title: Cabinet Mix for Parallel Feel
rules.description: Use Cabinet Mix control for subtle speaker emulation
rules.details: At 100% you get full cabinet character. At 50% you blend cabinet with direct signal. At 0% cabinet is bypassed entirely.

useCases.100%: Full amp simulation, realistic guitar tones
useCases.50-75%: Subtle speaker character on non-guitar sources
useCases.0%: Only stompbox effects, no cabinet filtering

rules.check: Cabinet character matches desired tone without overwhelming

rules.title: Output Gain Final Adjustment
rules.description: Master output gain is your final safety net
rules.details: After all processing, adjust output gain so the signal leaves Hardcore at appropriate level. This should be the LAST control you touch.
rules.target: Match input level or match next plugin's expected input
rules.check: Output meter shows healthy level (around -12 to -6 dBFS)
rules.violation: Output consistently clipping or too low
rules.solution: Adjust Output Gain to healthy level, revisit earlier stages if needed

rules.title: Avoid Digital Clipping
rules.description: Never allow signal to exceed 0dBFS inside Hardcore or at output
rules.details: Hardcore is not a true analog circuit. Digital clipping is harsh and undesirable. Even 'analog-modeled' distortion has limits.
rules.check: No red clipping indicators on any stage
rules.solution: Reduce gains at earlier stages, especially input and distortion drive

rules.title: Parallel Processing Gain Matching
rules.description: When using Hardcore on send track, ensure unity gain
rules.details: Set Hardcore internal mix to 100% wet. Control the blend using the send track fader and/or send level knob on source track.
rules.check: Processed signal at same level as dry when send at 100%
rules.violation: Can't achieve unity blend (too loud or too quiet)
rules.solution: Adjust Hardcore output level to match source track level

gainStaginWorkflow.step1: Set Input Gain to healthy level (0dB or source-dependent)
gainStaginWorkflow.step2: Add stompboxes one by one, adjusting their individual levels
gainStaginWorkflow.step3: Watch cumulative gain - reduce levels if stacking gain-heavy effects
gainStaginWorkflow.step4: Set Master EQ (minimal boosting, surgical cutting preferred)
gainStaginWorkflow.step5: Select appropriate Cabinet model and mix amount
gainStaginWorkflow.step6: Adjust Output Gain for final level matching

harshness-control.description: Guidelines for preventing and controlling harsh, unpleasant frequencies when processing with Hardcore

rules.title: Understand Harsh Frequency Ranges
rules.description: Harshness typically occurs in 2-5 kHz range
rules.details: The 2-5kHz region contains frequencies that can sound grating, fatiguing, or 'ice-picky' when exaggerated. Distortion and bright processing can push these over the edge.

frequencyCharacteristics.2kHz: Vocal presence, can become harsh if overdone
frequencyCharacteristics.3kHz: Attack and bite, easily becomes grating

rules.check: Listen for fatigue or discomfort during extended playback
rules.solution: Use Master EQ to gently reduce 2-5kHz if needed

rules.title: Distortion Amount vs. Harshness
rules.description: Higher distortion drive increases harshness non-linearly
rules.details: Distortion adds harmonics. As you increase Drive, you create more high-frequency harmonics which can accumulate into harshness.

driveThresholds.extreme: 85-100% - Extreme saturation, likely harsh without mitigation

rules.check: High drive settings (70%+) with bright tone = harshness risk
rules.solution: Combine high drive with darker tone or EQ cuts in 3-5kHz

rules.title: Multi-Effect Harshness Accumulation
rules.description: Harshness compounds when stacking multiple effects
rules.details: Each effect can add a small amount of edge. Chorus, flanger, phaser, and distortion all contribute. The cumulative effect can become harsh even if individual effects sound fine.
rules.cumulativeCheck: Bypass all effects, enable one by one, identify harshness source
commonCulprits: Flanger with high feedback + Bright cabinet
rules.solution: Reduce number of active effects or use darker cabinet/EQ

rules.title: Cabinet Selection for Harshness Control
rules.description: Cabinets act as final tone filters - choose wisely
rules.details: The cabinet is your last line of defense against harshness. Darker cabinets naturally roll off the frequencies that become harsh.

cabinetHarshness.cabinet2: LOW RISK - Rolled off above 6kHz, warm
cabinetHarshness.cabinet5: VARIABLE - Limited range cuts harshness but can sound boxy

rules.check: Does chosen cabinet smooth or exaggerate harshness?
rules.solution: Cabinet 2 or 4 for harshness-prone sources; Cabinet 1 only if source is naturally dark

rules.title: Master EQ as Harshness Filter
rules.description: Use Master 8-band EQ for surgical harshness reduction
rules.details: Bands 5 (1kHz), 6 (3kHz), and 7 (6kHz) control the harshness range. Gentle cuts here preserve clarity while removing grating edge.

eqStrategy.band5: Cut -1 to -2 dB if honk/boxiness present
eqStrategy.band6: Cut -2 to -4 dB for primary harshness control
eqStrategy.band7: Cut -1 to -3 dB for high-mid bite control

rules.technique: Start with -2dB cuts, A/B test, adjust by ear
rules.check: Harshness reduced but clarity maintained

rules.title: Pre-Distortion Filtering
rules.description: Remove harsh frequencies before distortion adds harmonics
rules.details: Distortion creates new harmonics from existing frequencies. If you distort a harsh source, you create MORE harshness. Filter first.
rules.check: Source sounds slightly dull before distortion, balanced after
rules.solution: Use Stompbox EQ before Distortion in the chain

rules.title: Modulation Effects and Harshness
rules.description: Chorus, flanger, and phaser can add edge
rules.details: Modulation effects create movement but can also add metallic or glassy character that contributes to harshness perception.

settings.flanger: Negative feedback (-20 to -50%) for hollow rather than metallic
settings.phaser: Fewer stages (2-4) for less resonant peaks

rules.check: Modulation adds width without metallic harshness
rules.solution: Reduce depth/feedback or move modulation earlier in chain

rules.title: The Lo-Fi Solution
rules.description: When harshness persists, embrace the lo-fi aesthetic
rules.details: Sometimes the source is naturally harsh. Rather than fighting it, use Hardcore to push into intentional lo-fi territory where harshness becomes character.
rules.useCase: When modern clarity is unattainable or undesirable

rules.title: Gain Staging Impact on Harshness
rules.description: Improper gain staging can create digital harshness
rules.details: Digital clipping and near-clipping levels create unpleasant, harsh distortion. Even 'analog-modeled' plugins behave badly when overdriven digitally.
redZones: Input gain pushing +12dB with hot source
Distortion Level at 100% with high drive
rules.check: No red meters at any stage
rules.solution: Reduce gains at earlier stages, maintain -6 to -12dB headroom

rules.title: Test at Multiple Volumes
rules.description: Harshness perception changes with playback volume
rules.details: Fletcher-Munson curves mean we perceive high frequencies differently at different volumes. A setting that sounds balanced at conversation level may be harsh at performance level.
testingProtocol: Test on different playback systems (headphones, monitors, earbuds)
rules.check: Harshness doesn't increase disproportionately at high volume
rules.solution: If harsh at high volume, reduce 3-5kHz regardless of low-volume impression

rules.title: Reference Track Comparison
rules.description: Compare your Hardcore settings to professionally mixed references
rules.details: Professional mixes rarely sound harsh. If your Hardcore-processed material sounds edgier than reference tracks, you have a harshness problem.
comparisonPoints: Snare drum attack - crisp but not painful
Vocal clarity - present but not grating
Overall mix - engaging but not fatiguing
rules.check: Your processed material matches professional harshness level
rules.solution: Reduce Master EQ 3-5kHz range until harshness matches reference

harshnessTroubleshooting.harshDrums: Reduce 3kHz (Band 6), Use Cabinet 2 or 4, Lower Distortion Tone
harshnessTroubleshooting.harshVocals: Cut 2-5kHz pre-distortion, Use Cabinet 2, Reduce Drive
harshnessTroubleshooting.harshGuitars: Check multiple distortion stacking, Reduce 3-4kHz, Darker cabinet
harshnessTroubleshooting.harshSynths: Often source-related - high-pass or use Cabinet 5 for limitation

universalHarshnessReducer.description: Gentle presence reduction suitable for most sources

sibilance-safety.description: Guidelines for controlling sibilance (harsh 's', 'sh', 't' sounds) when using Hardcore on vocals and bright sources

rules.title: Identify Sibilance Frequency Range
rules.description: Sibilance typically occurs between 5-10 kHz
rules.details: The 's', 'sh', 'ch', and 't' sounds contain strong energy in the 5-10kHz range. Hardcore's distortion and bright cabinets can exaggerate these frequencies.
rules.check: Solo vocals and listen for harsh 's' sounds
rules.solution: Target 6-8kHz range on Master EQ Band 7 (6kHz) and Band 8 (12kHz)

rules.title: Use Caution with Bright Cabinets on Vocals
rules.description: Cabinet 1 (Bright/Modern) extends highs to 8kHz+
rules.details: Cabinet 1 has strong 3-5kHz presence and extended treble. Combined with distortion, this can make vocals painfully sibilant.
rules.warning: Cabinet 1 + High Distortion + Vocals = Sibilance risk
rules.check: A/B test cabinet selection on vocal phrases with 's' sounds
rules.solution: Switch to darker cabinet or reduce high-end before cabinet

rules.title: Pre-Distortion EQ is Critical
rules.description: Distortion adds harmonics, exaggerating existing high frequencies
rules.details: If you distort a signal with existing sibilance, you create MORE sibilance through added harmonics. Use Stompbox EQ before Distortion to tame highs.
rules.check: Distortion on/off comparison - does it exaggerate 's' sounds?
rules.solution: Enable Stompbox EQ before Distortion, cut 8-10kHz range

rules.title: Master EQ De-Essing
rules.description: Use Master 8-band EQ for broad de-essing
rules.details: Band 7 (6kHz) and Band 8 (12kHz) control the sibilance range. Gentle cuts here can tame harshness without making vocals dull.

settings.alternative: Cut Band 6 (3kHz) by -2dB if sibilance is lower frequency

rules.check: Vocal 's' sounds are controlled but not lisping
rules.caution: Don't over-cut - vocals need presence and air

rules.title: Distortion Tone Control Strategy
rules.description: Distortion Tone control affects sibilance generation
rules.details: Positive Tone values (+10 to +50) emphasize high frequencies, potentially creating sibilance even in clean sources.
rules.check: Tone setting doesn't exaggerate 's' sounds
rules.solution: Reduce Tone setting or combine with high-frequency cuts

rules.title: Test with Sibilance-Rich Material
rules.description: Always test Hardcore settings with phrases containing 's', 'sh', 't'
rules.details: A setting that sounds great on 'oo' and 'ah' vowels may be painfully harsh on 'sassy sailors shoot ships'. Test comprehensively.
testPhrases: She sells seashells by the seashore
The sixth sheik's sixth sheep's sick
rules.check: All sibilant sounds are controlled, no single sound jumps out
rules.solution: Adjust settings until all phonemes sound balanced

rules.title: Post-Hardcore De-Esser Strategy
rules.description: Consider dedicated de-esser after Hardcore on vocal chain
rules.details: If Hardcore is essential for vocal character but creates sibilance, add a dedicated de-esser plugin after Hardcore in the chain.
rules.chainPosition: Source → Hardcore → De-Esser → Rest of chain
rules.check: De-esser catches what Hardcore exaggerates

rules.title: Drum Cymbal and Hi-Hat Control
rules.description: High-frequency drum elements also need sibilance management
rules.details: Cymbals and hi-hats contain sibilant-like energy in 8-15kHz range. Hardcore can make them harsh and splashy.
rules.check: Cymbals sound present but not painfully bright
rules.solution: Reduce treble in Master EQ or choose darker cabinet

rules.title: Mix Level Compensation
rules.description: Sibilance issues often worsen at higher mix levels
rules.details: An effect that sounds balanced at 20% mix may expose sibilance at 50% mix. Always check at your intended blend level.
rules.check: Test at actual mix level you'll use in production
rules.solution: Adjust Hardcore settings at intended mix percentage

rules.title: Automation for Problem Sections
rules.description: Automate Hardcore settings for sibilant passages
rules.details: If only certain words are sibilant, automate the Master EQ or Tone controls to reduce highs during those moments.
automationTargets: Master EQ Band 7 (increase cut during sibilance)
Cabinet Mix (reduce to blend in less cabinet high-end)
rules.check: Sibilant sections are controlled without affecting rest of vocal
rules.solution: Create automation clips for sibilant words/phrases

drumSafeChain: Consider: Less distortion on cymbal-heavy sections
